headline: New Hampshire heating-aid providers see more first-time applicants as oil costs rise
dek: Community-action agencies say more working families are seeking help, while federal forecasters expect heating-oil households to spend more this winter than last.
body: New Hampshire community-action agencies are seeing more residents seek heating assistance for the first time as a costlier fuel season approaches. Providers described a rise in new applicants and questions about overdue balances during a Monday roundtable in Concord, according to reporting by the [New Hampshire Bulletin](https://www.newsfromthestates.com/article/oil-prices-soar-more-nh-residents-fall-behind-their-heating-bills). The early applications are a warning that the state's fuel-assistance program is being asked to cover households whose budgets were already strained before the first sustained cold weather arrives.

The pressure is being amplified by the outlook for heating oil. The U.S. Energy Information Administration said Oct. 6 that homes primarily using heating oil are expected to pay about 21% more for the fuel this winter than last winter. EIA also forecasts roughly a 30% increase in heating-oil prices, partly offset by an expectation of milder Northeast weather. The agency said tight distillate markets are keeping oil costs elevated, while higher inventories are giving natural-gas customers a somewhat different price outlook. Those are national forecasts, not a promise about any individual New Hampshire delivery.

A separate estimate cited by the Bulletin, from the National Energy Assistance Directors' Association, puts the typical Northeast heating-oil season at about $2,300, or more than $500 above last year. The estimates use different methods and should not be added together: EIA is forecasting fuel spending for oil-heated homes, while NEADA is describing a regional seasonal-cost estimate. A household's actual bill will depend on the home's size and insulation, thermostat settings, equipment efficiency, weather and the price charged by its supplier.

The impact is already showing up at local agencies. Staff with Community Action Partnership Belknap-Merrimack Counties told the Bulletin that inquiries about overdue fuel accounts are running ahead of last year's pace. Southwestern Community Services reported many applicants who are working and new to the program. That does not establish how many households statewide are in crisis, but it does show that the higher costs are reaching beyond the residents who have traditionally used fuel assistance.

New Hampshire's program is the state version of the federally funded Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program, or LIHEAP. The [Community Action Partnership Hillsborough and Rockingham](https://www.caphr.org/services/fuel-assistance) program page says eligible homeowners and renters may receive grants from $188 to $2,500 for heating, with payments covering qualifying deliveries of oil, kerosene, propane, wood or coal from Oct. 1 through April 30. Electric and natural-gas assistance follows a different billing schedule. The benefit is assigned to the fuel vendor or, in some cases, the landlord; it is not a cash payment that a household can use for any expense.

The program is limited by eligibility and available funds. The Bulletin reports that New Hampshire generally serves households with income up to about 60% of the state's median household income. The community-action program says priority pre-applications for the 2026-27 season became available after July 1 for certain households, including older or disabled residents and families with young children, while other households could pre-apply after Sept. 1. Its page lists April 30, 2027, as the application deadline, but residents should confirm current income rules and local appointment requirements with their administering agency.

Federal action is still uncertain. U.S. Rep. Chris Pappas has proposed increasing LIHEAP support and expanding eligibility, according to his [Sept. 25 announcement](https://pappas.house.gov/media/press-releases/pappas-introduces-new-legislation-to-lower-energy-costs), but a bill or proposal is not the same as enacted funding. New Hampshire providers told the Bulletin they want more money and timely federal disbursements because assistance may not cover a full delivery, and one winter can require several deliveries.

For residents, the immediate decision is whether to apply before a tank or account reaches an emergency. The community-action agencies say people who are close to the income guidelines should apply and let the program determine eligibility; some income may be treated differently than a household's own calculation. The state's assistance can reduce a bill, but it cannot erase the exposure created by rising fuel prices. Whether Congress changes the federal program, and how severe the winter becomes, will determine how much of the gap families must absorb themselves.
author: NorthEast News Desk
seoTitle: New Hampshire heating aid demand rises as oil costs climb
seoDescription: New Hampshire fuel-assistance providers report more first-time applicants as EIA forecasts higher heating-oil costs for the 2026-27 winter.
